div.p: In this paper we present an integrated scheduling approach which allows to handle real-time task sets with d$ferent types of constraints and criticalness. Tasks are scheduled on-line in a dynamic environment based on the Earliest Deadline First algorithm. Schedulability conditions are derived for hybrid task sets consisting of hard periodic tasks and soft aperiodic activities, interacting through shared resources. Bounded blocking on exclusive resources is achieved by means of a dynamic resource access protocol which also prevents deadlocks and chained blocking. Aperiodic responsiveness is enhanced by an efJicient servicing technique which assigns a suitable deadline to each aperiodic request. Moreovel; the feasibility conditions are extended to handle tasks with deadlines dijferent than periods.

Concurrency control protocols for handling resources constraints have been proposed under the Rate Monotonic (RM) [ 141 and under the Earliest Deadline First scheduling algorithm (EDF) [5, 21, but without considering the presence of aperiodic tasks. On the other hand, several aperiodic service mechanisms have been proposed under RM [ 10,16, 1 1, 1,201 and EDF [17,8,18,19], but no resources constraints have been taken into account between periodic and aperiodic tasks. Some extension has also been done for considering periodic tasks with deadlines less than periods [ l , 201 and for accounting the cost of the interrupt handlers into the system [9]. However, no much work has been done for analyzing the schedulability of hybrid task sets of hard periodic tasks and soft aperiodic tasks which can interact through shared resources.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: This problem has been addressed by an off-line schedul-Predictable execution of real-time control applications requires the supporting operating system to handle tasks with different characteristics. For example, time critical activities should be implemented as hard periodic tasks and guaranteed in worst case conditions. Less critical realtime activities (called soft activities) do not need to be guaranteed; however, they should be executed as soon as possible without jeopardizing the guarantee performed on the hard tasks. If soft activities interact with hard tasks through shared resources, such an interaction has to be taken into account in the schedulability analysis. The problem becomes more complex if periodic tasks are permitted to have deadlines different than their periods and if peripheral devices may interrupt the processor at arbitrary instants.

In the real-time literature, several algorithms have been proposed for dealing with specific subproblems, but not sufficient work has been done for integrating tasks with several types of constraints, especially in dynamic environments. For example, Liu and Layland [ 121 found important results ing approach [6]. In this context, all types of constraints can be considered in a pre-runtime analysis, and an optimal (or sub-optimal) solution can be found for the scheduling problem. This method is very powerful, but it is not flexible enough for considering dynamic environments, where task arrivals are not known in advance. Recently, an hybrid method has been proposed for integrating on-line service of aperiodic requests with an off-line schedule of periodic tasks [7], but no interaction is possible between the two sets. The same problem has also been considered by a heuristic approach in the Spring kernel [ 151, but no schedu-Iability analysis is performed, and no optima1 solutions can be found.

In this paper, we address the problem of scheduling hard periodic and soft aperiodic tasks that may share resources used in exclusive mode in a dynamic environment, where tasks are scheduled based on their deadlines. Periodic tasks may also have relative deadlines different than their periods.

div.head: Accounting for shared resources
div.p: The schedulability analysis under resource constraints has been carried out assuming that a maximum blocking time Bi is experienced by each task ~i . Under the EDF scheduling algorithm, this can be achieved by using a resource access protocol, such as the Dynamic Priority Ceiling (DPC) [5] or the Stack Resource Policy (SRP) [2]. In particular, the SRP has been selected for its simplicity and generality.
According to this protocol, every hard (periodic and sporadic) task is assigned a static preemption level defined as
Every resource Rk is assigned a dynamic ceiling yk defined as Yk = max {n-i I T; can be blocked on &}. a A system ceiling is also defined as
Then, a job is not allowed to start executing until its priority is the highest among the active jobs and its preemption level is strictly greater than the system ceiling.

This protocol has several advantages. For example, it is suitable for both static and dynamic scheduling algorithms, it prevents deadlocks, bounds the maximum blocking times of tasks, reduces the number of context switches, and is very easy to implement. Moreover, the SRP ensures that once a task is started, it will never block until completion; it can only be preempted by a higher priority task. Using SRP, the maximum blocking time Bi that a job Ji can experience at its activation is equal to the duration of the longest critical section, among those that can block Ji (i.e., those belonging to tasks with preemption level lower than ri).
Notice that the maximum blocking time can easily be calculated as follows:

div.p: As observed before, the complexity of this schedulability test is pseudo-polynomial. Also notice that soft aperiodic tasks are not taken into account in this analysis, because soft tasks do not have deadlines and no preemption levels can be assigned to them. As a consequence, soft tasks cannot share resources with hard tasks, otherwise an unbounded priority inversion could occur. This problem is addressed in the next section.

div.head: Sharing resources between soft and hard tasks
div.p: If soft aperiodic tasks share resources with hard periodic tasks, the schedulability test expressed in Theorem 5 needs to be modified to take aperiodic service into account. The analysis is in general different from the case in which tasks are independent, since the aperiodic service policy may also affects the maximum blocking times of the tasks.

In order to let soft aperiodic tasks share resources with hard periodic tasks under the SRP protocol, each aperiodic request must be assigned a "fictitious" deadline, required for defining its preemption level. Moreover, the deadline must be assigned in such a way that the request can be scheduled by EDF without jeopardizing the guarantee performed on the hard tasks.

In the rest of this section, we first show a method for assigning "safe" deadlines to aperiodic tasks, so that the whole hybrid task set can be guaranteed even under resource constraints. Then we illustrate how these deadlines can be used to compute the preemption levels for the SRP protocol.

div.head: Assigning deadlines to soft tasks
div.p: An efficient method for assigning deadlines to soft aperiodic requests has been proposed by Spuri and Buttazzo in [ 191. In this work, the authors describe an algorithm, called Total Bandwidth Server (TBS), for enhancing the response time of aperiodic tasks in hard real-time environments. The name of the server comes from the fact that, each time an aperiodic request enters the system, the total bandwidth of the server (in terms of available processor time) is immediately assigned to it. This is simply done by assigning a suitable deadline to each request, which is then scheduled according to the EDF algorithm together with all the periodic and sporadic instances ready to execute. The assignment of the deadline is done to improve the aperiodic responsiveness, still maintaining the schedulability of periodic tasks.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper we addressed the problem of integrating resource constraints in the execution of hybrid task sets including hard periodic and soft aperiodic tasks. Schedulability conditions have been derived for the Earliest Deadline First algorithm, which has been extended to deal with periodic tasks having deadlines less than periods and sharing resources with soft aperiodic tasks. The analysis has been carried out by considering that resources are accessed through the Stack Resource Policy and aperiodic tasks are serviced by the Total Bandwidth Server. Interrupt handling cost has also been considered in the feasibility conditions in the particular case in which aperiodic tasks do not interfere with hard tasks.

The complexity of the analysis proposed in this paper is pseudo-polynomial, because the problem has been shown to be NP-hard [3]. As consequence, the resulting schedulability tests might be too costly for providing an on-line guarantee. Nevertheless, it is important to point out that this method can be used to perform an off-line guarantee of all critical periodic and sporadic tasks and to reserve sufficient bandwidth to serve aperiodic tasks on-line.

This approach permits the definition of timing and resource constraints, without explicitly imposing the release times, as typically done in off-line scheduling approaches. In this way we take the advantage of dynamic scheduling for handling aperiodic requests on-line and automatically reclaiming resources whenever possible.
Work is in progress for extending the schedulability analysis of hard tasks interacting with soft aperiodic tasks in the presence of interrupt handlers.
